title: Free-body diagram (FBD)
body: A single-object or single-system diagram that shows every force the environment exerts on it, drawn as separate straight arrows starting on the center-of-mass dot.

items.label: Dot
items.meaning: Represents the object or system's center of mass; all force arrows originate here.

items.label: Force arrows
items.meaning: Each force exerted on the object by the environment is its own straight arrow starting on the dot and pointing in the direction of the force.

items.label: Same-direction forces
items.meaning: Forces pointing the same way are drawn side by side, not overlapping.

items.label: Whole forces only
items.meaning: Depict the forces themselves, not force components.

items.label: Coordinate axis
items.meaning: Choose one axis parallel to the direction of acceleration (e.g., parallel to an incline) to simplify translating the diagram to algebra.

caution: Label gravity F_g, F_G, W or mg; 'G' or 'g' alone is not accepted. Show only forces exerted on the object, not a separate 'net centripetal force' arrow.
ced_evidence: 2.2.B.2-2.2.B.4 and boundary statement: 'individual forces represented on a free-body diagram must be drawn as individual straight arrows, originating on the dot'

title: Tension
body: Tension is the macroscopic net result of the forces that segments of a string, cable, chain, or similar system exert on each other in response to an external force.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.3 'Tension is the macroscopic net result of forces that segments of a string, cable, chain, or similar system exert on each other'

title: Action at a distance is gravitational only
body: In AP Physics 1, the only interaction between objects or systems at a distance is the gravitational force.
ced_evidence: 2.3 boundary statement: 'The interaction between objects or systems at a distance is limited to gravitational forces in AP Physics 1.'

title: Ideal string
body: An ideal string has negligible mass and does not stretch under tension, so the tension is the same at all points within it.
caution: A string with nonnegligible mass can have different tension at different points (e.g., a hanging chain has greater tension toward the top); AP Physics 1 asks only for a qualitative description of this.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.3.i-ii 'An ideal string has negligible mass and does not stretch when under tension'; 'The tension in an ideal string is the same at all points within the string'

title: Ideal pulley
body: An ideal pulley has negligible mass and rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction.
ced_evidence: 2.3.A.3.iv 'An ideal pulley is a pulley that has negligible mass and rotates about an axle through its center of mass with negligible friction'

title: Direction of acceleration and when velocity changes
body: A system's center-of-mass acceleration points in the same direction as the net force on it, and its velocity changes only if a nonzero net external force is exerted on it.
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.2 'in the same direction as that net force'; 2.5.A.3 'will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system'

title: Newton's second law
ced_evidence: 2.5.A.2 'acceleration of a system's center of mass has a magnitude proportional to the magnitude of the net force exerted on the system'

title: Weight
caution: On a free-body diagram, label weight F_g, F_G, W or mg; 'G' or 'g' alone is not accepted.
ced_evidence: 2.6.A.3 'The gravitational force exerted by an astronomical body on a relatively small nearby object is called weight.'

title: Apparent weight
body: The magnitude of a system's apparent weight is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on it, which differs from the gravitational force when the system is accelerating.
caution: A system appears weightless when no forces act on it or when gravity is the only force on it, not because gravity is absent.
ced_evidence: 2.6.C.1 'The magnitude of the apparent weight of a system is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the system.'

title: Direction of kinetic friction
body: The kinetic friction force on each surface is exerted opposite to that surface's motion relative to the other surface, and it does not depend on the contact surface area.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.1.i 'exerted in a direction opposite to the motion of each surface relative to the other surface'

title: Normal force
body: The normal force is the perpendicular component of the force a surface exerts on an object in contact with it, directed away from the surface.
caution: Because it points away from the surface, it need not point up; for example, at the top of a vertical loop it points downward.
ced_evidence: 2.7.A.2.ii 'Normal force is the perpendicular component of the force exerted on an object by the surface with which it is in contact; it is directed away from the surface.'

title: Period of uniform circular motion
caution: Valid only for constant speed (uniform circular motion).
ced_evidence: 2.9.A.5.iii 'For an object traveling at a constant speed in a circular path, the period is given by the derived equation'; 2.9.A.5.ii T = 1/f
